To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the minimum stimulus-onset-asynchrony required to produce the illusion of rigid rotation increases as a linear function of the difference in orientation between two views of the object; and (b) the slope of that function is virtually constant across changes in object size.
the apparent velocity of rigid rotation is bounded by a velocity constant and that the value of the velocity constant is a function of the size of the stimulus object.

the minimum stimulus-onset-asynchrony required for rigid rotation is a linearly increasing monotonic function of the angular distance between two views, and that the slope of the function is invariant with variation in object size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the visual perception of rigid rotation.
the perception of motion in space.
the nature of the visual system's representation of motion and the processes by which this representation is constructed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the apparent angular velocity (or, in the case of the rigid rotation illusion, the apparent angular velocity as a whole) is limited by a velocity constraint, which is independent of the object's size.
the velocity of the object is a linearly increasing and increasing function of the velocity of the velocity of velocity.
the apparent velocity of rigid rotation is bounded by an upper velocity limit that is constant for a given observer and that this velocity limit is independent of the size of the stimulus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual system is capable of computing the angular velocity of the whole, but not of the parts.
the visual system does not compute a rigid rotation of the stimulus as a whole, but rather computes a rigid rotation of a set of local features, which are then combined in some way.
apparent rigid rotation is not a simple consequence of motion parallax, but is constrained by the velocity of the object.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the appearance of rotation is not simply a consequence of a linear velocity constraint, but is a more complicated function of the stimulus.
apparent rotation of an object is constrained by an apparent angular velocity of that object.
the apparent angular velocity is limited by the maximum rate at which the visual system can update the orientation of an object.
